closures.explanation: `increment` keeps access to `count` after `makeCounter` has returned. Each call to `makeCounter` creates a new `count` variable, so `counterA` and `counterB` track their counts independently. Nothing outside the closure can change `count` directly.

promises.explanation: A Promise represents a value that will be available later. `resolve` fulfills it and `reject` marks it as failed. `.then` runs on success, `.catch` handles any rejection earlier in the chain, and `.finally` runs either way.

array methods.explanation: `filter` keeps elements that pass a test, `map` transforms each element, `reduce` combines elements into one value (always pass an initial value), and `some` checks whether at least one element passes. `filter` and `map` return new arrays and don't change `orders`.

recursion.explanation: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller piece of the problem. Here, each nested array is summed by a recursive call. The loop ending (no more elements) acts as the base case, so the recursion always stops.

async/await.explanation: `async` functions always return a Promise. `await` pauses the function until the Promise settles, letting you write asynchronous code top to bottom. Use `try...catch` to handle rejected Promises. Callers still need `await` or `.then` to get the result.

objects.explanation: Objects store key/value pairs and can hold methods that use `this`. The spread syntax makes a shallow copy: top-level properties are copied, but nested objects are still shared references, so changing `shallowCopy.author` also changes `book.author`.
